text: […] Their garments, sandals, and coverings remained untouched, just as they had been sewn when they came out of Egypt. The rock itself prefigured Christ, as the divine apostle says: ‘They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.’ To show that the water was nourishing, listen to what a certain wise man writes: ‘They drew honey from the rock for the wonder-worker in the wilderness.’ Do you see why he called it nourishing honey? The psalmist says likewise, ‘He fed them with honey from the rock’; and [in the Song of Deuteronomy it says], ‘oil from the flinty rock.’ [All bear witness that the water had the power to serve as nourishment for every kind of food.] After the whole generation of the disobedient had died, and their offspring had sprung up and grown to maturity, Moses alone remained from that generation. God said to him, ‘Teach the children [of Israel] about their disobedience to my commandments [and remind them of my wonders], and write this song for them: “Give ear, O heaven, and I will speak; let the earth hear the words from my mouth.”’ [They are to learn this song; whoever does not learn it by heart and keep it on the lips will be cut off from the people. Instead, let the children of Israel write this song and carry it in their mouths, so that through it they may learn the wonders I did among them and how often their fathers embittered me.] ‘And I, because of the oaths I swore to Abraham, did not fail to do good to them. Teach them all my commandments, everything I charged you on the mountain.’ Moses spoke all these words to the people. Concerning the death of Moses: Moses said to Joshua son of Nun, ‘Let us go up the mountain.’ When they had gone up, Moses saw the promised land and said to him:

‘Go down to the people and announce to them that Moses has died.’ Joshua went down to the people, while Moses had reached the end of his life. Samael [whose name is printed in the edition as Samouel] tried to bring Moses’ body down to the people so that they might deify him. But Michael, the commander of God’s host, came by God’s command to take and restrain the body. Samael resisted him, and they fought. The commander grew angry and rebuked him, saying, ‘May the Lord rebuke you, devil!’ Thus the adversary was defeated and fled. The archangel Michael laid Moses’ body where Christ our God had commanded; [no one saw Moses’ burial]. Concerning Joshua son of Nun: Joshua son of Nun took up the Lord’s people and came to the Jordan, intending to enter the promised land. There was a city near the Jordan, to the west, whose tower was built entirely of stone [called lodestone]. When Joshua heard of it, he sent spies to view the city and reconnoitre it for him. The spies entered, but the people of Jericho recognized them, so they fled. They came to an inn and found Rahab the prostitute. They begged her to hide them. She asked, ‘Who are you?’ They answered, ‘We are Jews [Israelites].’ Rahab said, ‘I have heard that you have a great God and are servants of the great God. Go your way without fear, for I will turn the people of Jericho away from you.’ Rahab led them out through the wall and showed them the way. When the people of Jericho came, she pointed them along another road, saying that the spies had gone that way. Thus the spies escaped. When they returned, they reported everything to Joshua son of Nun [how the townspeople had recognized them

and how they had been saved by Rahab the prostitute]. When they had come near the Jordan, the Lord said to Joshua son of Nun, ‘Today I will exalt you before all the children of Israel, so that they may know that, just as I was with Moses, I will also be with you. Now command the priests who carry the ark of the covenant of the Lord to enter and stand in the Jordan.’ The Jordan could not be crossed on foot, for it was in flood. The priests came and stood in the middle of the Jordan’s waters. The river was full over all its banks, as it is during the wheat harvest. The river is formed from the Sea of Tiberias on one side and the Lake of Gennesaret on the other; one part is called the Yōr and the other the Dan, and when the two join downstream they are called the Jordan. When the priests of God who carried the ark entered, the water was cut off. The water flowing from upstream stood in a heap, far away at Adam, a city as far as the region of Kiriath-jearim; the water flowing downstream ran to the Arabah Sea, the Sea of Salt, until it was completely spent. All the people crossed the Jordan on dry ground, and then they began the war against Jericho. Concerning the appearance of the commander-in-chief: the people of Jericho began to wage war, and battle took place every day. The fighters could not defeat the people of Jericho, and Joshua was distressed. One day, while Joshua was encouraging the people during battle, the commander-in-chief of the Lord appeared to him, standing on the right side of the battle with his sword drawn in his hand. Joshua saw him, approached him, and asked, ‘Are you one of us, or one of our

enemies?’ The commander-in-chief answered him: ‘I am the commander-in-chief of the Lord; I have now come to help you.’ Joshua fell down and worshipped him, saying, ‘My lord, what do you command your servant?’ The commander-in-chief of the Lord said, ‘Remove the sandal from your foot, for the Lord God will hand the people of Jericho over to you. Take nothing from them [not even a single coin; keep away from their goods], lest you worship their gods and set yourself against the law of the Lord, for God’s law brings salvation.’ The commander-in-chief said, ‘Let the priests take seven trumpets and circle the walls of Jericho for seven days; let them sound the trumpets around Jericho, and the walls will fall.’ Then the commander-in-chief departed. The priests did as commanded, and on the seventh day the walls of Jericho collapsed and the whole city fell. When this had happened, Joshua said to the people, ‘Take nothing from this city—not even a single coin—and let no one escape, except Rahab the prostitute, who saved the spies.’ A man named Achar, a Jew by birth, was found. He had stolen bracelets and many gold pieces shaped like tongues. Thus they took the city of Jericho. Concerning Jericho and Ai: after taking Jericho, they went up into the hill country to a small stronghold called Ai. The men of Ai ambushed them and killed thirty armed warriors. Joshua was distressed and fell on his face. The angel of the Lord said to him, ‘Look and search the people of the Lord: they have broken your command because of Achar, and for this reason the men of Ai have become strong.’ Joshua searched and found that Achar had stolen the forbidden things.

Joshua ordered Achar to be stoned, and all Israel stoned him. They burned his household and his livestock [and destroyed all his descendants]. After carrying out the punishment, they went up and took Ai, destroying it and sparing nothing there except the animals. From Jericho, Rahab the prostitute alone was spared. The psalmist remembers this, saying, ‘I will remember Rahab and Babylon among those who know me’ [that is, those who fear me]. When the Canaanites heard that the Jews were advancing, they melted with fear; then the saying was fulfilled: ‘All the inhabitants of Canaan melted away,’ for the Canaanites lived in that land. When the Gibeonites heard that God’s people were coming against them, they said: ‘Their God divided the sea and brought them through; he routed Amalek and wiped them out; he humbled the Assyrians; he destroyed the Moabites; he ruled over Edom; he made the land of Midian subject; he laid waste to Uz; he utterly wiped out the Ammonites; he devastated the Salt Sea region; and he cut off the Jordan and brought them through on dry ground. No river, sea, army, or wall of Jericho can stand against them; even the walls have fallen by the power of their God.’ When the Gibeonites heard all this, they devised a scheme. They put on filthy clothes and ragged tunics, took old wineskins, sour wine, cracked bread, and worn sandals, then disguised themselves and came to the camp, to the leaders and Joshua son of Nun. Falling before him, they said, ‘My lords, we have come to pay you homage; do not destroy us.’ The leaders asked, ‘Where have you come from?’ They answered, ‘We have come from a distant land, seeking peace with you. Look at these old tunics we wear: we put them on unworn. These loaves were fresh when we took them. We have come seeking peace.’ The leaders and Joshua son of Nun believed them and made peace with them as

they had requested, and were deceived, for the Gibeonites were nearby though they had said they came from far away. The Gibeonites went home without fear. The Jews went out to plunder the surrounding cities and came to Gibeon. The Gibeonites who had come seeking peace went out to meet them. The Jews recognized them and asked, ‘Is this your city?’ They answered, ‘Yes.’ They said, ‘Why did you deceive us, saying that you came from a distant land?’ All the people rose up against Joshua and the leaders, saying, ‘Why did you not ask God? Instead, you acted foolishly and made a reckless treaty.’ The Gibeonites came to meet Joshua and fell at his feet. Joshua said to them, ‘You deceived us, saying that you came from a distant land, though you live near us. Now, by our oath, we will not harm you, but you shall serve the camp of the children of Israel as water-carriers and woodcutters.’ So he made them servants. A wise man writes about this: ‘Rise up and fight as Joshua son of Nun did: conquer the passions of the flesh and the Gibeonites—that is, the deceitful thoughts—always overcoming the evil thoughts that deceive us. Just as the Gibeonites deceived Joshua son of Nun and the leaders of the Jews, so an evil thought deceives us into doing wrong while we do not realize it. Therefore the wise man prays to conquer deceitful thoughts.’ Concerning Aedor: Joshua son of Nun ruled for twenty-one years, and after him the elders ruled. The kings of the Persians came, fought, and conquered them, and the Jews became tributaries of the Chaldeans. A man named Aedor arose among the Jews. Seeing that his fathers had been enslaved by the Chaldeans, he began to seek the liberation of his homeland. He said to the Jews, ‘Make me your leader, and I will free our homeland from the Chaldeans.’ The Jews answered him, ‘We will make you our ruler. Take gifts and go to Gog, king of the Persians.’

for Gog then ruled the Persians, Chaldeans, Medes, and Gazarenes, and held power over the Jewish people. Aedor took the gifts and went to Gog, king of the Persians. He bowed and presented the gifts, saying, ‘My lord, these have been sent to you by your servants, the Jews.’ Gog was pleased by the gifts and welcomed him warmly. Aedor lodged in the king’s camp, for he had brought three thousand battle-ready warriors with him. They received their provisions from Gog’s palaces. Aedor wished to return home and said to the king, ‘I have a private matter to tell you, king of the people.’ Gog replied, ‘Let us go into the inner part of the palace, and you can tell me.’ When they were alone, Aedor secretly drove a sword into the king’s belly, split him open, and threw him to the ground, dead and speechless. He went out, locked the door behind him, and told the attendants, ‘The king is asleep. He ordered me to lock the door so that he would not be disturbed.’ Aedor then went to the Jews and said, ‘Prepare yourselves; let us plunder the Persians and escape from here.’ They prepared and began plundering the Persians. When Gog’s officials saw what was happening, they broke open the palace doors [and] found Gog lying dead. Aedor took much booty and went with the Jews to Jerusalem. David remembered this when he cursed his enemies. They were destroyed by Aedor. How pleasing to God is a sacrifice, a deed worthy of praise.

‘Present her as a daughter [to Jephthah, pure and undefiled, and sacrifice the passions of your flesh like an offering to your Lord].’ Concerning Jephthah: Jephthah was of the tribe of Dan and was driven out of his tribe because he was illegitimate: his mother had slept with her own slave and bore him. The twelve tribes of Israel did not mingle with one another, but each tribe held its own inheritance. Therefore the psalmist says, ‘A measuring line of inheritance,’ and elsewhere, ‘within the measuring line of the inheritance.’ Driven out from his tribe, Jephthah went up to the mountain and lived there alone. The children of Israel were subdued by the nations and had no respite. The Israelites were distressed, having no ruler, and they came to Jephthah asking him to join their alliance. He refused, saying, ‘You drove me from my tribe, so I cannot join you in war.’ They agreed under oath to make him ruler over the whole people if he fought and won the war. Jephthah heard the words of the people and their leaders and went out to war. As he set out, they swore that they would not take the enemy’s spoils. Jephthah also swore: ‘If anyone comes out to meet me when I return victorious, I will offer that person as a sacrifice to the Lord my God.’ He went to war and won. As he returned, his daughter heard that her father was coming back victorious and went out to meet him. When Jephthah saw his daughter, he began to lament.
